8 Related Work

8.1 Foundation Models as Embodied Agents

Large language and vision-language models have long been used to bring semantic knowledge into robot control, but mostly at the level of high-level reasoning. SayCan [68] grounds an LLM’s proposals in the affordances of a pretrained skill library, and Inner Monologue [66] closes the loop by feeding success detection and scene descriptions back to the planner. Code as Policies [98] prompts the model to write programs that call perception and control APIs, while VoxPoser [65] and ReKep [64] have it compose 3D value maps or relational keypoint constraints that a motion planner then optimizes. Gemini Robotics-ER [48] extends this line with a model trained specifically for embodied reasoning. In all of these systems the foundation model specifies what to do, while a predefined skill set, planner or separately trained controller decides how. We instead ask whether a frontier model can act as the controller itself, emitting end-effector actions in closed loop from its own observations.

A second line of work, which has grown rapidly in 2026, borrows the harness paradigm of coding agents [74, 110] and holds that embodied performance depends as much on the infrastructure around the model as on the model itself. Some harnesses redesign the action interface: RoboDawn [54] and Show-Harness [28] expose discrete, semantically meaningful motion commands that a frozen VLM can issue directly, and Robo-Harness K1 [97] equips the model with calibrated perception tools such as depth, object tracking and grasp hypotheses. Others focus on context and verification: Thea [145] maintains a scene graph as persistent context and treats evaluation outcomes as exit codes, and Zetta [36] evolves code-based runtime critics and recovery skills around a frozen base policy. Guava [101] distills a frontier-model harness into a compact open model, while RHO [39], HARBOR [96] and EmbodiedSWE [130] use coding agents offline to build policy repositories, automate reinforcement-learning pipelines, or write programs against the full simulator state. Related studies examine how agents adapt from in-context experience [7, 142] and how reasoning latency interacts with a changing environment [153, 180]. Our ablation in Sec. 3 complements these system-level proposals by isolating the contribution of individual harness components, namely the action interface, subagent roles and memory, under a common protocol.

8.2 Robot Policy Learning

The dominant paradigm for robot control learns a policy from demonstrations. Early large-scale efforts such as BC-Z [71] and RT-1 [17] trained language-conditioned policies on large collections of teleoperated episodes, while Implicit BC [44], BeT [128], ACT [178] and Diffusion Policy [30] introduced action representations better suited to multimodal, high-precision behavior, and 3D Diffusion Policy [170] further conditions on point clouds. These policies are typically trained and evaluated per task, and most established manipulation benchmarks, including several used in this report, were designed around this setting (Sec. 5).

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit semantic knowledge from web-scale pretraining by fine-tuning a vision-language model to output actions. RT-2 [185] first demonstrated this transfer, OpenVLA [83] provided an open-source counterpart, and Octo [52] and RDT [103] trained generalist policies on cross-embodiment data such as Open X-Embodiment [120] and DROID [79]. The π\pi series [14, 122, 13] pairs a VLM backbone with flow-matching or tokenized action experts and reaches open-world generalization in unseen homes, while GR00T N1 [114] and Gemini Robotics [48] extend the recipe to humanoids and to frontier-scale backbones. Recent systems such as Xiaomi-Robotics-0 [18] and MolmoAct2 [41] target real-time execution and deployable action reasoning. Grounding language in physical action nonetheless remains data-hungry, which has motivated the alternatives below.

World action models (WAMs) start instead from video or world-model backbones and predict how the scene will evolve together with the actions that produce it [148, 129]. UniPi [37] generates videos and recovers actions with an inverse-dynamics model, GR-1 and GR-2 [154, 22] pretrain on large-scale video, and Seer [139], VPP [60], UVA [94] and UWM [184] couple future prediction and action generation more tightly through predictive representations or joint diffusion. In 2026 this family has scaled rapidly. Cosmos Policy [82] and LingBot-VA [93] turn large video foundation models into policies, Fast-WAM [169] finds that most of the benefit comes from video modeling during training rather than from imagining the future at test time, and DreamZero [166] reports that WAMs generalize zero-shot to new tasks and environments substantially better than VLAs. A robustness study on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0-Plus likewise finds WAMs more robust to visual and language perturbations [176].

The most recent systems blur the boundary between the two families. Motus [10] and BagelVLA [61] train unified models in which understanding, video-generation and action experts share attention, VLA-JEPA [137] augments a VLA with a latent world model, and π0.7\pi_{0.7} [123] conditions its action expert on subgoal images produced by a world model. Despite their differences, all of these approaches learn a policy from robot data. We ask the complementary question of how far a general-purpose frontier model can go as a policy without benchmark-specific policy training, and our harness ablation (Sec. 3) also invokes a VLA (π0.5\pi_{0.5}) as a callable tool.

8.3 Embodied Benchmarks

LIBERO [99] remains the most widely used simulation suite for language-conditioned manipulation. LIBERO-Plus [42] and LIBERO-PRO [183] perturb its scenes and instructions to expose brittleness and memorization, and LIBERO-Long++ and LIBERO-Ultra-Long [162] stress visual clutter and chains of 9 to 16 skills. SIMPLER [95] evaluates real-world policies in matched simulation, RoboCasa365 [112] scales simulated household tasks for training and benchmarking generalist robots, RoboDojo [26] unifies simulated and real-robot evaluation of generalist policies, and RoboLab [161] adds high-fidelity scenes with controlled perturbations. For dexterous control, Bench2Dex [163] benchmarks visuo-tactile bimanual manipulation across hand designs, and DexJoCo [144] provides task-oriented dexterous tasks covering tool use, bimanual coordination and long-horizon execution in MuJoCo.

For navigation, Room-to-Room [3] established instruction following on a discrete navigation graph, VLN-CE [87] moved the task to continuous environments with low-level actions, and LHPR-VLN [134] extends it to long-horizon, multi-stage instructions.

Household benchmarks broaden the scope further. BEHAVIOR and BEHAVIOR-1K [135, 90, 8] derive everyday activities from human needs and evaluate full-length household tasks. Housekeep [76] and TIDEE [127] test commonsense tidying without explicit instructions, HAZARD [182] places agents in dynamically changing environments, PARTNR [21] evaluates multi-agent planning, and EmbodiedBench [159] and IS-Bench [106] evaluate multimodal LLM agents on vision-driven tasks and on interactive safety, respectively. Simulation platforms such as Genie Sim [167] continue to raise the fidelity of these evaluations.

Benchmarks lose discriminative power as leading systems saturate them [80, 119]. Evaluation of language agents has responded with harder tasks [20, 138, 4] and with outcome-based protocols in which an agent acts in an environment by any means and is scored on the result [74, 155, 110], a protocol that EmbodiedSWE [130] brings to robotics. As discussed in Sec. 5, most of the embodied benchmarks above were designed for policies trained by imitation, and we argue that general-purpose agents call for a different design.

8.4 Empirical Studies of Frontier Models in Embodied Settings

Each generation of frontier models has prompted empirical studies of its embodied abilities. Shortly after the release of ChatGPT and GPT-4V, Vemprala et al. [141] and Wake et al. [143] examined how these models could be prompted to plan and program robot tasks, and NavGPT [181], MapGPT [24] and Open-Nav [124] studied zero-shot vision-and-language navigation with LLMs reasoning over textual or map-based descriptions of the scene. GPT-4 also generated dense end-effector trajectories and replanned with external visual feedback [89]. CaP-X [46] compared action abstractions, interaction modes, and perceptual grounding, exposing the dependence of model performance on supplied tools and interfaces. Our previous study [19] evaluated GPT-5 on eight spatial-intelligence benchmarks under a unified taxonomy and found unprecedented strength that nonetheless fell short of human performance across a broad range of tasks. The present report extends that effort from spatial to embodied intelligence, and from perception and reasoning to closed-loop control.

The release of GPT-6-Astra [117] set off a wave of such studies within weeks. In navigation, two evaluations on R2R-CE [34, 33] find that GPT-6-Astra rivals or surpasses prior zero-shot and supervised methods from monocular RGB input, yet still struggles to turn correct local judgments into reliable route execution and stopping decisions. In manipulation, Zhang et al. [174] report that GPT-6-Astra ranks first among public entries on the RoboDojo leaderboard while other frontier LLMs succeed in fewer than 2% of trials, but also that one-shot demonstrations lower rather than raise its success rate and that real-robot trials had to be halted because of unsafe actions. Astranomy [158] compares direct, agentic, and policy-assisted control, while Ditto-Bench [104] examines action interfaces, memory, and reasoning effort in contact-rich manipulation. Other studies examine how demonstration formats and accumulated interaction memory affect in-context adaptation [100, 29, 165, 168], the reuse of body knowledge and prior experience together with sim-to-real transfer [57], direct manipulation on LIBERO [35], token-efficient agents that compose classical primitives with VLA calls [132], and GPT-6-Astra’s capabilities as an embodied policy more broadly [47, 164, 67]. RoboMME studies examine full-history direct control [72] and hierarchies combining Astra planning, learned execution, and lightweight monitoring [23]. Real-robot studies demonstrate coding-agent control and correction [73], while broader evaluations expose reliability gaps and substantial execution time and inference costs [5, 121, 177, 109]. Vals Robo-bench [140] incorporates inference delays through continuously running physics and wall-clock budgets. The Embodied Agent Arena [62] compares seven VLMs on 1,000 cases drawn from 32 benchmarks and finds that GPT-6-Astra excels at precise estimation and contact localization but not at coordinating goal-directed sequences, Rasheed et al. [125] observe a similar split between semantic and metric-geometric tasks across computer vision, and RoboQuest [102] examines evidence acquisition and exploration stopping decisions. RoboHarm [136] reports that GPT-6-Astra completed 60 of 100 deliberately harmful robot-arm trials and refused only two.

These studies typically examine one benchmark family, one capability or one harness at a time, and their conclusions do not always agree: demonstrations lower GPT-6-Astra’s success on RoboDojo in Zhang et al. [174], yet RoboICL [100] reports gains when demonstrations are combined with interaction memory, and RoboDawn [54] reports similar gains from one-shot demonstrations with a frozen VLM. Our study differs in evaluating manipulation and navigation benchmarks under a single protocol, ablating harness design, validating on real robots, and drawing on these results to propose principles for the next generation of embodied benchmarks.

9 Full Simulation Results

9.1 LIBERO-PRO

Tasks and demonstrations. LIBERO-PRO [183] applies task-preserving perturbations to the four LIBERO suites and separates each suite into Task and Swap variants. We evaluate the complete official benchmark: eight suites, ten tasks per suite, and ten fixed initial states per task, for 800 episodes in total. Before evaluation, we freeze a package selected by the exact base task, combining matching Task/Swap task-family notes with global strategy, perception, verification, and recovery notes distilled from a separate public exploration phase. The package contains no reported evaluation trajectory or outcome, current initial state, or reusable pixels, coordinates, object suffixes, or action sequences. We refer to our configuration as GPT-6-Astra + ICL. It uses maximum reasoning effort and direct robot control, with both the VLA and SAM3 disabled. All 800 episodes are valid and uncensored.

Observation and control settings. GPT-6-Astra observes calibrated RGB images from a fixed third-person agentview camera and the Panda wrist camera (native ×256256\!\times\!256 observations, with ×10241024\!\times\!1024 inspection renders), together with the measured end-effector pose and gripper state. The agent interface also provides calibration-based pixel back-projection into the current scene; LIBERO-PRO does not expose object poses or evaluator diagnostics to the planner. The underlying action is the benchmark’s seven-dimensional Panda OSC-pose command at 20 Hz: three translational components, three axis–angle rotational components, and one gripper command. The interface compiles model-selected Cartesian motion, wrist-rotation, and gripper primitives into these actions. A unit translational or rotational component corresponds to 5 cm or 0.5 rad, respectively.

Budgets and continuation. The standard 1×1\times boundary is the first of 10,000 environment steps or 100 planner turns. An unsuccessful episode then continues from the same simulator state and planner conversation to a cumulative 10×10\times environment-step budget; the continuation is not terminated by the 100-turn 1×1\times cap. The frozen 1×1\times outcome is never replaced by the continuation. Table 3 reports success rate (SR) for every paired Task/Swap base task, the four family aggregates, and all 800 episodes, while integrating prior agentic and policy-based methods at their reported suite-level granularity.

Results and comparison. At 1×1\times, GPT-6-Astra + ICL succeeds in 786 of 800 episodes (98.25%), exceeding the published RPent/GPT-6-Astra baseline with low reasoning [175], the strongest prior result, by 5.62 percentage points. It obtains 99–100% SR on six suites; the remaining errors concentrate in Long Task (97%) and Long Swap (90%). Continuing to the cumulative 10×10\times boundary raises the result to 794/800 (99.25%), including 99% on Long Task and 95% on Long Swap. Table 3 also reports the mean test-time token and wall-clock cost at both boundaries.

9.2 LIBERO-Long++ and LIBERO-Ultra-Long

Tasks and demonstrations. LIBERO-Long++ and LIBERO-Ultra-Long [162] evaluate compositional manipulation under visual clutter and reordered skill chains. Long++ contains six scenarios in their original and reordered forms, yielding 12 configurations; Ultra-Long contains three scenarios under the original ordering and two reorderings, yielding nine configurations. We follow the released protocol and run ten independent bare-random resets per configuration, for 120 Long++ and 90 Ultra-Long episodes. Before testing, we construct one frozen package per composite task solely from the released atomic-skill training split, which contains 4,050 trajectories (150 per atomic skill; 351,999 transitions). The package summarizes canonical, geometric-variation, and recovery examples as phase, contact, verification, and failure cues with labeled agent-view and wrist-view contact sheets. It contains no evaluation rollout, initial state, reward, success label, or test-specific coordinates. We refer to our configuration as GPT-6-Astra + ICL. It uses maximum reasoning effort and direct robot control, with both the VLA and SAM3 disabled.

Observation and control settings. GPT-6-Astra observes calibrated RGB images from a fixed third-person agentview camera and the Panda wrist camera (native ×256256\!\times\!256 observations, with ×10241024\!\times\!1024 inspection renders), the measured end-effector pose and gripper state, and the released ordered-skill and instance-pose feedback used by our LiLo adapter. Calibration-based pixel back-projection supplies current-scene 3D geometry. The underlying action is the benchmark’s seven-dimensional Panda OSC-pose command at 20 Hz: three translational components, three axis–angle rotational components, and one gripper command. The agent interface compiles model-selected Cartesian motion, wrist-rotation, and gripper primitives into these actions. A unit translational or rotational component corresponds to 5 cm or 0.5 rad, respectively.

Budgets and continuation. The standard 1×1\times step budgets are 600 or 800 steps on Long++ and 1,800, 2,000, or 3,200 steps on Ultra-Long. Success rate (SR) requires completion of the entire ordered chain within this boundary. Average progress (AP) is the fraction of the uninterrupted correct skill prefix completed at the same boundary. An unsuccessful episode continues from the same simulator state and planner conversation to a cumulative 10×10\times step budget; the 1×1\times outcome and prefix snapshot remain frozen. There is no separate planner-turn cap; a 12-hour planner wall-clock guard handles infrastructure censoring but does not change the environment-step budget. Prior work does not report an agentic method under this protocol. Table 4 reports every task and compares GPT-6-Astra + ICL with LiLo-VLA and two learned-policy baselines in the corresponding ordering-level aggregate rows.

Results and comparison. At 1×1\times, GPT-6-Astra + ICL achieves 97.5% SR and 99.2% AP on LIBERO-Long++, and 82.2% SR and 95.7% AP on LIBERO-Ultra-Long, exceeding LiLo-VLA by 15.5 and 38.2 percentage points in SR, respectively. The cumulative 10×10\times results reach 100.0% SR/AP on Long++ and 98.9% SR with 99.4% AP on Ultra-Long. Macro-averaged over the nine scenarios, the corresponding results are 92.4%/98.1% at 1×1\times and 99.6%/99.8% at 10×10\times. Table 4 also reports one-time preparation cost per composite task and mean test-time cost per episode.

9.3 RoboDojo

Tasks and demonstrations. We refer to our experiment as GPT-6-Astra + ICL. We evaluate all 42 RoboDojo tasks across 5 groups [26]. Generalization, Precision, Long-Horizon and Memory contain 34 tasks in total; Open contains 8 tasks. Each task uses layout_id=0--4, giving 210 evaluation episodes. We fix seed=0; each layout is initialized with env.reset(seed=[layout_id]). For each task in Generalization, Precision, Long-Horizon and Memory, GPT-6-Astra studies 10 demonstrations of that task. The 8 Open tasks have no task-specific demonstrations and share one study of 340 demonstrations from the other 4 groups, 10 per task.

Observation and control settings. Our RoboDojo experiments use the dual-arm ARX X5 robot, and GPT-6-Astra receives 640×480640\times 480 RGB images from head, left-wrist and right-wrist cameras, measured joint positions, gripper states and end-effector poses. Privileged information is withheld: object poses, depth images, segmentation masks, contact information, hidden simulator state, task source code and evaluator diagnostics. For each arm, GPT-6-Astra outputs a target end-effector position (x,y,z)(x,y,z) in meters in the environment coordinate frame, a target orientation as a unit quaternion (w,x,y,z)(w,x,y,z), and an open or close gripper command. Each target differs from the current measured pose by at most 5 cm in position and 0.35 rad in orientation. Inverse kinematics converts these end-effector targets into joint targets, with each control step limiting end-effector translation to 2 cm, rotation to 0.1 rad and each joint’s rotation to 0.05 rad. Control runs at 25 Hz; an action request can repeat a target for 1–10 control steps. After each action request, GPT-6-Astra uses the returned images and measured robot state to choose the next action.

Budgets and continuation. We evaluate GPT-6-Astra + ICL with the 1×1\times and 10×10\times step limits. Each task has a standard control-step limit BB ranging from 200 to 1,900 steps, with evaluation limits of BB and 10​B10B, respectively. We first run each episode for up to BB control steps, or until earlier termination, and measure the 1×1\times result from this initial execution. If the episode has not terminated, we continue the same episode up to a total of 10​B10B steps and record the 10×10\times result. Execution ends when the simulator terminates the episode or GPT-6-Astra stops.

9.4 RoboLab

Benchmark and tasks. RoboLab [161] evaluates task-generalist manipulation policies in high-fidelity simulation. Its RoboLab-120 task library comprises 120 language-conditioned tasks organized along three competency axes: visual recognition, relational understanding, and procedural reasoning. Tasks span three difficulty levels and include object selection, spatial rearrangement, stacking, and reorientation. The benchmark supports evaluation of policies trained on real-world data without requiring co-training on simulation data.

Policies and evaluation metric. Table 6 compares GPT-6-Astra with nine baselines spanning vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs). We report success rate (SR), expressed as a percentage, together with policy type and model size. Baseline results are taken from the official RoboLab leaderboard for the default language instructions; each listed baseline is evaluated over 1,200 episodes. Model sizes follow the reported parameter counts. These published results provide reference points for the agent evaluation; the table does not establish a comparison at matched inference cost.

Results. Under the standard (1×1\times) budget, GPT-6-Astra achieves a success rate of 57.1%, exceeding all baselines listed in Table 6. It exceeds FLUX 3 Action, the strongest listed baseline at 42.9%, by 14.2 percentage points. Among the listed VLAs, π0.5\pi_{0.5} performs best at 28.0%, trailing GPT-6-Astra by 29.1 points. The aggregate results show an advantage for GPT-6-Astra on this comparison, while task-level outcomes would be needed to identify which competency axes account for the difference.

9.5 Bench2Dex

Tasks and demonstrations. We evaluate all 26 Bench2Dex [163] tasks across 12 arm–hand embodiments under Full randomization (inv_cov, unseen split). The paired cohort contains three fixed episodes per task (indices 5–7), totaling 78 episodes. Preparation uses all 100 released seen-split replay recordings per task, including rendering variants of shared motion trajectories. Demonstrations expose four-camera RGB, active-joint positions, and demonstrated joint targets. Discrepancies between recorded and current task instructions are flagged, with the current instruction remaining authoritative.

Observation and control settings. GPT-6-Astra receives stereo left/right and wrist left/right RGB images at 640×480640\times 480, measured active-joint positions, robot kinematics, and camera calibration. Camera intrinsics and camera-to-robot-base transforms are obtained from the simulator after randomization. We supply kinematics and calibration as setup information readily accessible in a calibrated robotic deployment, consistent with our objective of assessing GPT-6-Astra’s capabilities given available test-time information. Object states, depth, segmentation, contacts, and evaluator feedback are excluded. Actions are absolute active-joint targets executed at 20 Hz, with three 60 Hz physics steps per target. GPT-6-Astra chooses the action-chunk length, and our wrapper adds no interpolation or clipping.

Budgets and continuation. The standard budget follows the benchmark, Bt=⌈1.5​Et/3⌉B_{t}=\lceil 1.5E_{t}/3\rceil, where EtE_{t} is the expert reference duration in physics steps. BtB_{t} ranges from 593 to 1,542 control steps. SR uses official stable-success early stopping, with a 0.5 s dwell except for Faucet Cup Water Fill, which requires 3 s. Only standard-budget timeouts receive additional interaction up to a total of 10​Bt10B_{t}, while successes and other terminal failures retain their outcomes. Because the original 1×1\times runs were already complete, we reconstruct timeout endpoints using the original reset configuration and exact recorded-action replay, then resume the original episode context. Replay must match archived numerical states and boundary stage histories within fixed tolerances. The continuation additionally permits an observation-grounded explicit give-up, counted as failure.

Results and comparison. GPT-6-Astra achieves 25.6% SR at 1×1\times, comparable to the published π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline of 25.5%, and reaches 61.5% at 10×10\times, an increase of 35.9 percentage points. The baseline uses 50 episodes per task, evaluated separately from our three episodes per task. Reported test-token counts in Table 7 are lower bounds because usage accounting is partial; tokens-per-success values derived from these counts are therefore also lower bounds and do not establish a cross-benchmark token-cost ranking.

9.6 DexJoCo

Tasks and demonstrations. We evaluate all 11 DexJoCo [144] tasks (six single-arm and five bimanual) under rand_full, using five fixed test seeds per task (100000–100004; 55 episodes). This regime randomizes object placement and table height, external camera pose, lighting, and table texture, while dynamics randomization is disabled. For each task, preparation has access to 100 released rand_full replay recordings through a restricted reader that exposes robot proprioception, demonstrated actions, timestamps, and selected RGB videos. GPT-6-Astra also receives the pinned robot model. Each task’s resulting notes, reference examples, and control utilities are frozen as one package before testing.

Observation and control settings. At test time, GPT-6-Astra receives 640×640640\times 640 RGB from one external camera and one wrist camera for single-arm tasks, or two wrist cameras for bimanual tasks. Public robot state contains end-effector pose and 16 hand-joint values per arm (23 or 46 values). Object state, depth, contacts, rewards, and success flags are withheld. Actions specify absolute world-frame end-effector position and rotation vector plus 16 hand-joint targets per arm (22 or 44 values), executed at 30 Hz. GPT-6-Astra may submit 1–30 actions per decision. The interface converts rotation vectors to the quaternion format expected by the simulator.

Budgets and continuation. DexJoCo’s task-specific standard limits range from 1,000 to 1,500 action steps. Success is determined by the simulator’s task-specific success flag. Only episodes that exhaust the standard limit without a terminal outcome continue toward 10​B10B, for which a fresh GPT-6-Astra session resumes the same live simulator instance with the episode’s observation and action history. No reset or trajectory replay is used for these continuations. For click_mouse, we reproduce the benchmark client’s 30-step initial alignment and count those steps against the task budget.

Results and comparison. GPT-6-Astra achieves 78.2% SR at 1×1\times, exceeding the published π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline of 40.3% by 37.9 percentage points, and reaches 87.3% at 10×10\times, a further increase of 9.1 percentage points. The baseline reports results over three training seeds with 50 test episodes per task per seed, while GPT-6-Astra uses five test seeds per task.

9.7 LHPR-VLN

Benchmarks and tasks. LHPR-VLN [134] evaluates long-horizon vision-language navigation. Given a global natural-language instruction, the policy must reach multiple navigation goals in a strictly specified order. Following these instructions requires visually grounding successive goals, tracking completed stages, and using earlier observations to guide subsequent movements.

Evaluation subset. The official unseen test split contains 205 episodes across 27 scenes. Many episodes contain subtask target objects that are not visible along the reference trajectories. We manually checked target visibility along each episode’s reference trajectory and retained an episode only when every subtask target object was visible. The resulting subset contains 114 episodes across 25 scenes, with two to four goals per episode. The complete retained episode list appears below.

Protocol and metrics. Each episode starts in a fresh session with the global instruction and a frozen ICL workspace containing exploration notes, code, and observations from training scenes that do not overlap with the test scenes. Test episodes do not share interaction history. During navigation, the policy receives three RGB views at a resolution of 366×366366\times 366, facing left, forward, and right at +60∘+60^{\circ}, 0∘0^{\circ}, and −60∘-60^{\circ}. Available actions are 0.25 m forward motion, 30∘30^{\circ} left or right turns, and STOP. Three consecutive blocked forward actions trigger a random turn and a forward action, both counted toward the action budget. Ground-truth trajectories, target coordinates, and scores are withheld. To submit a goal, the policy issues STOP, which advances the stage regardless of success. A submission succeeds within 1 m geodesic distance of the original target or a matching target object in the specified room. Environment feedback identifies the current stage without revealing submission success. The 1×1\times and 10×10\times settings allow 500 and 5,000 actions per sequence. Extended evaluation retains successful 1×1\times outcomes and evaluates only initially unsuccessful episodes with the larger budget, preserving earlier scores when they are higher. Metrics are averaged over all 114 episodes. SR measures full-sequence success. ISR, CSR, and CGT describe individual-goal and sequential success, with definitions in the table note.

Results. GPT-6-Astra Max + ICL achieves 21.05% SR at 1×1\times, compared with 5.26% for Claude Code Opus-5 and 2.44% for FantasyVLN in Table 9. Extended evaluation raises SR to 28.95%, increasing completed episodes from 24 to 33. ISR rises from 54.68% to 62.87%, while CSR and CGT improve by 8.42 and 8.67 percentage points. Average test-time token consumption increases from 1.317 M to 2.587 M, or 1.96×1.96\times the initial cost.

Discussion. Full-sequence success remains below 30% under extended evaluation despite individual-goal success above 60%. Reaching some goals improves ISR, whereas SR requires every goal to be completed in order. A failed submission advances the sequence irreversibly, making goal verification and progress tracking consequential. Aggregate scores alone do not establish how much either contributes to the remaining failures. Baseline comparisons do not control for inference cost, and the reported token consumption should be considered alongside success rates.

Episode IDs. Each batch/index pair below identifies an episode as batch_b_episode_e, where bb is the batch number and ee is the listed episode index.

Batch 1: 2, 10, 19, 20, 55, 56, 60, 61, 62, 65, 81, 82, 84, 94, 103, 119, 128, 130

Batch 2: 1, 17, 20, 35, 52, 54, 69, 78, 85, 87, 88, 99, 103

Batch 3: 10, 24, 26, 36, 44, 46, 63, 69, 83, 86, 91, 97, 101, 103, 106, 107, 112

Batch 4: 31, 32, 36, 58, 66, 68, 110, 111, 112, 114

Batch 5: 3, 4, 7, 16, 21, 28, 38, 40, 45, 52, 53, 64, 72, 74, 75, 86, 88, 100

Batch 6: 34, 37

Batch 7: 13, 47, 56, 66, 74, 82, 83, 85, 99, 120, 123, 146, 160

Batch 8: 5, 30, 63, 66, 77, 82, 85, 100, 112, 115, 134, 141, 146, 154, 156, 161, 166, 180, 191, 205, 206, 211, 223

9.8 VLN-CE

Benchmarks and tasks. VLN-CE [87] evaluates instruction-guided navigation in continuous indoor environments. Given a natural-language route instruction, the policy must navigate from a specified starting pose to a single goal and stop. This requires grounding landmarks, tracking progress along the route, and choosing movements from visual observations without a predefined navigation graph.

Evaluation subsets. R2R [3] uses the 100-episode val-unseen subset from Open-Nav [124], which covers 10 scenes and is also adopted by SmartWay [131] and AgentCanvas [1]. For RxR [88], we select 100 English guide episodes from the val-unseen split of 3,669 English episodes across 11 scenes, matching the R2R subset’s episode counts in each of the same 10 scenes. With seed 0, we draw 20,000 stratified 100-episode subsets and retain the candidate with the smallest sum of two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov distances to the full English split for instruction word count and reference-path length. We then attempt 60,000 random within-scene episode replacements, accepting a change only if it reduces this sum. Instruction length is the whitespace-separated word count, and reference-path length is the sum of Euclidean distances between consecutive reference waypoints. The complete episode lists for both subsets appear below.

Protocol and metrics. Each episode starts in a fresh session with a frozen ICL workspace prepared using training scenes that do not overlap with the test scenes. Test episodes do not share interaction history. Observations contain a single forward-facing RGB image at 512×512512\times 512 resolution. Forward actions move 0.25 m. R2R uses 15∘15^{\circ} left or right turns, while RxR uses 30∘30^{\circ} turns and permits 30∘30^{\circ} upward or downward camera tilts. Ground-truth routes, goal coordinates, and evaluation scores are withheld. STOP terminates the episode and succeeds within 3 m geodesic distance of the goal. The 1×1\times and 10×10\times limits are 500 and 5,000 actions. Extended evaluation is applied to initially unsuccessful episodes. Reported extended results retain prior successes and the better per-episode value of each metric. Metrics are averaged over each 100-episode subset. NE is the final geodesic distance to the goal. OS is the oracle success rate, measuring whether the trajectory ever enters the 3 m success region. SR measures successful completion, and SPL [2] weights success by path efficiency. nDTW [69] measures alignment with the reference trajectory using normalized dynamic time warping.

Results. Extended evaluation raises SR from 80% to 88% on R2R and from 82% to 90% on RxR, adding eight successes per subset in Table 10. SPL improves by 8.51 and 7.91 percentage points, respectively. NE decreases from 3.45 m to 2.34 m on R2R and from 2.08 m to 1.36 m on RxR. R2R OS rises from 84% to 91%, while RxR nDTW increases from 77.85% to 82.98%.

Discussion. On R2R, OS exceeds SR by three percentage points under extended evaluation, identifying episodes that reach the goal region without stopping successfully. The RxR nDTW gain indicates closer alignment with reference routes. SPL remains below SR on both datasets, indicating that successful outcomes can still involve detours. Our results cover 100 episodes per dataset. Differences in episode coverage, observation access, and inference budgets limit direct comparisons with the listed baselines.

9.9 SIMPLE

Tasks and evaluation scope. SIMPLE [152] evaluates humanoid loco-manipulation on a Unitree G1 with two Dex3 hands. Our study uses the six-task evaluation set reported in Table 1 of the benchmark paper: XMovePick, BendPick, Handover, Tabletop, XMoveBendPick, and PickBetweenTables. Each task has three difficulty levels: L0 varies table texture and distractor type and placement; L1 adds extreme lighting changes; L2 further perturbs the target object’s initial position. With 10 released evaluation instances per task–level, this set contains 180 candidate episodes. Outcome coverage differs across the four GPT-6-Astra settings (zero-shot or ICL, at 1×1\times or 10×10\times), as specified below.

Coverage and comparison subsets. At the standard (1×1\times) budget, zero-shot (ZS) evaluation has complete outcomes for five tasks (XMovePick, BendPick, Handover, Tabletop, and XMoveBendPick), totaling 150 instances. Four of these tasks also have complete ICL outcomes, forming Common-4: XMovePick, BendPick, Handover, and Tabletop, with 120 instances. Cross-budget comparisons use Matched-8, the eight task–level combinations with complete outcomes in all four settings: XMovePick L0–L2, BendPick L0–L1, and Tabletop L0–L2, totaling 80 instances across three tasks. PickBetweenTables has only partial, outcome-selected coverage and is included solely in the reference aggregates, outside both comparison subsets.

Demonstration preparation. For task-level in-context learning (ICL), GPT-6-Astra explores the released training demonstrations through an information-bounded reader and compiles task notes, reference numerical data, image indices, and runnable helpers into a single hash-frozen package; the same package is shared across L0/L1/L2, every test episode starts from a fresh session, and no model weights are updated. Preparation accesses 99–100 released demonstrations per task; XMoveBendPick has no ICL package and is reported zero-shot only.

Observation and control settings. At test time GPT-6-Astra receives a head-mounted left RGB image (typically 640×360640\times 360), a 32-column robot-interface state, the task text, and the current episode’s history. It is additionally given nominal robot metadata (static URDF, joint order, and limits), robot-only forward/inverse kinematics, and NumPy/SciPy code tools; object pose, contacts, and online scoring feedback are withheld. Actions are continuous physical chunks of shape (T,36)(T,36)—finger and arm joint angles, torso roll/pitch/yaw, base height, base translation (vx,vy)(v_{x},v_{y}), a turn flag, and a target yaw—with the chunk length TT chosen by the model. Each action row is executed at 50 Hz by the task-specific official System 0 controller: the decoupled whole-body controller for the Teleop tasks, and the Ψ0\Psi_{0}/AMO motion-planning path for BendPick and Tabletop [151, 91]. The simulator is paused during inference, so reported action steps exclude thinking time.

Budgets and scoring. The standard (1×1\times) per-episode action budget is 800 steps for XMovePick, Handover, Tabletop, and XMoveBendPick, 400 for BendPick, and 1,200 for PickBetweenTables; the extended budget is 10×10\times. The Matched-8 comparison includes only complete task–level cells; partial results elsewhere use judged denominators, excluding unknown outcomes. Tabletop 1×1\times outcomes are thresholded from the 10×10\times trajectories, and one operator-stopped ICL episode (L2/E01) is counted as a failure by an explicit reporting rule. PickBetweenTables is an outcome-selected successful subset scored with a revised release metric. It is included only in the Six-task totals, which are provided for reference, and excluded from both the Matched-8 comparison in Table 11 and the Common-4 comparison in Table 12. Compute, sensing, tool access, inference latency, and rendering hardware are not matched across systems, so the comparison is descriptive rather than cost-controlled.

Results on the shared complete subset. Table 11 reports per-level success and two aggregate columns. The Matched-8 total compares all four GPT-6-Astra settings and the published baselines on the same 80 instances defined above. The subset is selected by completeness, not by success rate. On this subset, zero-shot success rises from 65/80 (81.3%) at 1×1\times to 79/80 (98.8%) at 10×10\times, while ICL rises from 77/80 (96.3%) to 79/80 (98.8%); both Ψ0\Psi_{0} [151] and DreamZero achieve 74/80 (92.5%) at 1×1\times. Thus, ICL improves standard-budget performance by 15.0 percentage points on this subset, while both GPT-6-Astra settings reach the same extended-budget success rate. These results describe the shared complete subset and do not estimate performance on excluded task–level cells. The Six-task total retains all judged outcomes for reference only: task coverage and denominators differ across rows, and the ICL aggregate covers five tasks because XMoveBendPick has no ICL package.

Standard-budget ICL and efficiency. Table 12 separately compares zero-shot and ICL at 1×1\times on the four common tasks (XMovePick, BendPick, Handover, and Tabletop), where all 120 episodes are judged in both settings. This is a broader subset than Matched-8 and is used only for the standard-budget comparison. GPT-6-Astra reaches 85/120 (70.8%) zero-shot and 109/120 (90.8%) with task-level ICL, a 20.0-percentage-point gain; the latter is comparable to the published Ψ0\Psi_{0} result of 108/120 (90.0%), and the one-case difference does not establish statistical superiority. Spatial generalization (L2) remains the main weakness at 1×1\times: ICL is 39/40 at both L0 and L1 but 31/40 at L2. On the 81 episodes solved in both settings, ICL reduces mean action steps from 376.9 to 210.4 (44.2%), while mean test token consumption rises from 2.64M to 6.40M. Mean test wall-clock time falls from 47.0 to 31.4 minutes; preparation additionally costs 8.34M tokens and 90.4 minutes per task, paid once. These cost figures use the matched-success set and should not be interpreted as measurements on the Matched-8 subset.

9.10 BEHAVIOR

Benchmarks and tasks. BEHAVIOR-1K [90] is a household embodied-AI benchmark covering 1,000 everyday activities grounded in human needs. Built on the OmniGibson simulator, it supports realistic interactions with rigid objects, deformable objects, and liquids. Its long-horizon activities require navigation and manipulation to achieve task-specific goal conditions.

We evaluate on all 100 tasks from the BEHAVIOR-1K 2026 Challenge, using public-test episode 0 with rollout seed 0 for each task and performing a single evaluation rollout per task instance. We retain the benchmark’s default R1Pro dual-arm mobile manipulator, with the arm-controller modification described below. Each rollout starts from the official task-instance initialization and proceeds through closed-loop interaction conditioned on head-mounted and bilateral wrist RGB-D observations, robot proprioception, and the task instruction. The simulator operates at 30 native steps per second, and each model-issued action can be repeated for 1–100 simulation steps. A rollout terminates upon environment termination, exhaustion of the official task-specific step budget, or an explicit agent finish call. Following the official evaluator, the step budget is set to 1.5 times the task’s mean human-demonstration length.

Protocol and Metrics. We use GPT-6 Astra with maximum reasoning effort for both demonstration-based in-context learning and evaluation. During the ICL stage, all official training data are provided including RGB videos, actions, proprioceptive states, and annotations. We adopt a 21-dimensional action interface, consisting of three base-control values, four torso joint targets, two six-dimensional absolute end-effector pose targets, and two gripper commands. Each end-effector target specifies a position and axis-angle orientation in the robot’s current base frame, which the official inverse-kinematics controller translates into arm motion. For consistency with this interface, demonstration arm commands are converted from joint-space targets to end-effector poses using the official forward-kinematics implementation.

We assess performance using the official evaluator, reporting binary task success, final predicate-based Q-score, simulator step count and simulated time, and base and end-effector travel distances together with their official human-normalized counterparts. Model token usage and wall-clock durations for individual stages are recorded separately to characterize computational cost.

Results. Across the 100 evaluation rollouts on the BEHAVIOR-1K 2026 Challenge, our method successfully completes 37 tasks, achieving an overall task success rate of 37%.

Other Discussion.The aggregate task success rate increases from 1% with the 23-dimensional joint-space interface to 37% with the 21-dimensional end-effector-pose interface. This substantial improvement is consistent with the hypothesis that task-space action representations better align language-model planning with robotic execution. By specifying the desired position and orientation of each end effector, the model can express manipulation intent directly while delegating joint-level kinematic computation to the official controller.

Qualitative inspection of the trajectories suggests that the model can extract procedural knowledge from demonstrations, identify task stages, and adapt its plans based on visual feedback. However, failures due to imprecise grasp alignment, arm collisions, navigation obstructions, and ineffective recovery strategies highlight persistent challenges in contact-rich manipulation. Taken together, these findings suggest that action representation plays a critical role in embodied task performance, but do not establish that high-level reasoning alone is sufficient for reliable robotic manipulation.

10 Harness Ablation Study

All experiments are evaluated on 42 tasks of RoboDojo [26] under a consistent evaluation protocol, with three evaluation runs per task using different seeds, except for ICL, which follows Table 5. We report both task scores, which capture partial task completion, and success rates (SR), which measure full task completion. Performance is further evaluated across five dimensions: Generalization, Precision, Long-Horizon, Memory, and Open. We additionally report the average token consumption per episode, including both input and output tokens from GPT-6-Astra and auxiliary agents, in millions (M), as a proxy for inference cost. Unless otherwise specified, each ablation is compared against baseline followed by our RoboRSI [118] to isolate the impact of individual design choices.

10.1 Agent Components

We evaluate four components individually: (i) a planning subagent that decomposes tasks into subgoals and completion criteria, with its outputs incorporated into the main agent’s context; (ii) an execution subagent that generates EEF actions from the main agent’s subgoals; (iii) a feedback subagent that evaluates execution outcomes and suggests continuation, adjustment, or retry; and (iv) history compression that retains the latest four turns and consolidates earlier interactions into a rolling summary capped at 2,000 tokens.

This study investigates how different agent components affect the embodied performance of GPT-6-Astra and whether increasing agent complexity consistently improves task execution. As shown in Table 13, introducing a feedback subagent yields the largest improvement, increasing the average score by 7.22 points and the success rate by 9.16 percentage points, with only a 7.03% increase in token consumption. History compression improves the score by 5.25 points and the success rate by 5.55 percentage points while reducing token consumption by 66.41%, demonstrating benefits in both performance and efficiency. The planning subagent provides a smaller overall score improvement of 3.25 points at a 15.63% increase in token consumption, although its substantial gain in the Memory category indicates that its benefits vary across task categories. In contrast, the execution subagent reduces the score by 1.22 points at approximately the same token cost as the baseline. These results suggest that effective agent design depends on how additional reasoning supports task execution, rather than on the number of components alone.

Feedback and history compression offer complementary benefits: explicit outcome evaluation improves task performance with a modest increase in token consumption, while compressing earlier interactions improves performance and substantially reduces context overhead. These findings motivate further investigation of structured execution memory and targeted verification mechanisms for tracking task progress and failures. Future harness design should assess additional components by their contributions to both task performance and total token consumption.

Findings

  • •

    Re-planning from feedback. When the receiving bowl is displaced by contact, GPT-6-Astra detects the change, raises the container and realigns before placing it (run 3, 07:06–10:40); after an empty grasp it re-grasps the cloth (folding run 2, 12:46–17:21).

  • •

    The prompt shapes the strategy. Unless alternative grasp points are named, GPT-6-Astra keeps trying to grasp a cup by its handle even when the pose is awkward or unreachable.

  • •

    Insertion is limited by observation and reachability. The pins and the socket are poorly visible, and poses that would reveal them are limited by joint reachability. Reorienting the initially upward-facing plug for insertion can also bring the arm close to its joint limits.

  • •

    Folding is judged without a shared criterion. An operator judges success from the final cloth state: a smaller, layered cloth packet remaining on the table after release, without requiring perfectly flat or aligned folds. All three reported trials met this practical criterion, although wrinkles and uneven edges remain (Fig. 13, B1). One run reached the 60-minute limit and was subsequently accepted based on its final state. Since the success criterion was not standardized across platforms (App. 11.2), the reported folding success rates are not directly comparable.

‡Judged on the Warm-button press. The wash cycle did not start in either run, which we attribute to the washer: it requires the Start button to be pressed shortly after Warm, and it showed an unexpected fault code in one run.  §0 of 4 and 1 of 4 flowers placed; both runs ended by a torso over-temperature fault.  The last six tasks are tabletop manipulation runs.

Findings

  • •

    Self-built context. GPT-6-Astra discovers the robot’s interfaces itself and records discrepancies with the documentation, such as a chassis message type that differs from the vendor guide.

  • •

    Contact without force sensing. GPT-6-Astra uses joint-effort change as a contact signal and approaches in small steps, and when reflective button surfaces corrupt the wrist depth, it cross-checks several depth patches against RGB.

  • •

    Long runs meet hardware limits. As a task proceeds, some runs hit hardware over-temperature faults that significantly affect completion; we regard this as a limitation of hardware reliability rather than of GPT-6-Astra.

Visualization

11.8 Wheeled Mobile Manipulator — AgileX Tracer + xArm7: Navigation and Search

Setting

Robot AgileX Tracer 1.0 mobile base with a UFactory xArm7
Cameras given to GPT-6-Astra Forward-facing RealSense D455 on the arm, uncalibrated, 1280×\times720 RGB
Action interface Three navigation waypoints per decision, followed by a waypoint controller (cruise 0.7 m/s); the pose is estimated by integrating the commanded velocity, with no odometry, SLAM or collision detection
Harness gpt-6-astra through the OpenAI API; each decision receives the latest RGB frame (downscaled to 640 px width) and returns the next waypoints
Budget and success rule No fixed time limit; runs last 0.2–8.3 min and end when the model reports completion or being blocked, on a timeout, or by operator interruption. A person scores each trial afterwards: it is a success only when the instructed physical goal and its spatial constraints are achieved and the model reports completion; all other trials count as failures

Context provided

  • •

    Task instruction and RGB input only: no robot model, SLAM or collision detection, and no demonstrations.

Tasks and results

Task (instruction given to GPT-6-Astra) Trials Success Wall-clock time
Pass the blue chair on the left, then approach the wooden box 5 2 0.5–3.6 min
Pass through the tripod–table gap, then approach the door 4 2 2.5–8.3 min
Approach the black monitor on the left 4 3 0.7–2.8 min
Find the person at the door on the right 5 2 1.2–3.0 min
Find the vacuum machine 5 0 0.2–1.1 min

Findings

  • •

    Losing track of progress. The robot loses its heading and, in some trials, forgets that it has already reached the goal area.

  • •

    Over-checking constraints. When told to pass a chair on the left, GPT-6-Astra repeatedly confirms the side instead of progressing toward the goal, and loses its way in some trials.

  • •

    No recovery after collisions. After a collision GPT-6-Astra almost never plans a recovery trajectory.

Visualization

11.9 Humanoid — Unitree G1: Tabletop Manipulation and Locomotion

Setting

Robot Unitree G1 humanoid (29 body DoF) with two Wuji Gen-1 dexterous hands; the right thumb is mechanically frozen, and waist, legs and body height are locked during manipulation
Cameras given to GPT-6-Astra Head-mounted Azure Kinect, RGB only; depth is recorded but neither given to the model nor used as a collision guard. Measured robot state is additionally available through tools
Action interface Manipulation: move_arms (14 absolute arm-joint targets in radians, clamped to joint limits and interpolated by the offboard arm controller) and set_hands (binary open/close profile per hand, no individual-finger, grip-width or force control; hands driven by the onboard Jetson). Locomotion: turn_to_heading (IMU yaw feedback), walk_forward (fixed 0.15 m/s for a commanded duration, at most 1.5 s per step) and stop, executed by the vendor high-level controller; GPT-6-Astra never commands leg joints, and no translational odometry is available to the policy
Harness Tool calls through the OpenAI Responses API (gpt-6-astra, reasoning effort max, mode pro, store=false); model calls, tool calls and camera frames are archived
Budget and success rule Six retained runs, three per task; manipulation and locomotion use different tool sets and are evaluated separately. No common 60-minute cutoff applies: both successful manipulation runs exceeded one hour. A person judges the binary outcome from third-person video after the run, separately from the model’s completion statement; the requested ∼\sim10 cm stopping distance is approximate and the final gap was not independently measured. Operator emergency stop throughout; the locomotion runs additionally use a slack safety-gantry strap

Context provided

  • •

    Task instruction, embodiment description, tool schemas, joint limits, camera placement, binary hand open/close profiles, locomotion and safety constraints, RGB observations, robot-state feedback, and the current run’s interaction history.

  • •

    No demonstrations, no demonstration-derived ICL package, and no semantic pick, place or navigation primitives; every motion is chosen by the model, one tool call at a time.

Tasks and results

Task (instruction given to GPT-6-Astra) Trials Success Wall-clock time
Pick up the blue plush toy and then drop it back onto the table 3 2 74:31; ∼\sim87:47
Turn, walk to directly in front of the table and stop about 10 cm from it without touching it† 3 3 8–13 min

† The locomotion instruction was given in Chinese; the wording above is a translation. Wall-clock times are listed for the two successful manipulation runs; per-run details below.

Run Outcome Tool calls Image calls Elapsed time
pickRun1 Failure 29 14 —∗
pickRun2 Success 74 36 ∼\sim87 min 47 s
pickRun3 Success 65 32 74 min 31 s
walkRun1 Success 18 9 12 min 49 s
walkRun2 Success 12 6 8 min 13 s
walkRun3 Success 13 7 10 min 12 s

∗ Elapsed time unavailable from the archived records.

Manipulation succeeds in 2/3 trials and locomotion in 3/3, giving 5/6 overall. The failed manipulation run drops the toy off the table, and recovery is not completed within the fixed-body workspace. With three trials per task, these results establish feasibility rather than reliability.

Findings

  • •

    Observation-conditioned approach under a safety constraint. In walk run 1, GPT-6-Astra shortens successive forward commands from 0.8 s to 0.5, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.15 s after fresh images, and all three locomotion runs stop at a self-estimated 0.15–0.20 m rather than 0.10 m, citing the no-contact requirement. This shows conservative progress assessment, not metric stopping accuracy.

  • •

    Valid joint targets do not guarantee faithful execution. In pick run 3, all 26 arm motions return stalled_short_of_target (18) or timeout (8), with median final tracking error 0.07065 rad and maximum 0.1904 rad, yet the human-labelled outcome is a success: useful motion occurs without meeting the joint-target criterion. GPT-6-Astra notices the discrepancies and adjusts, but reliable error compensation is not established.

  • •

    Slow supervision remains costly on hardware. Across 108 archived API calls, median request latency is 24.84 s, and API request wall time accounts for 88.8–91.7% of elapsed run time; image capture takes 4.5–9.0%. The remainder includes tool execution and harness overhead and is not a direct measure of physical motion time. Both successful manipulation runs last over an hour.
